title: Can Claude Write Slow AI? The Results
coverage: expanded selected original paragraphs with speaker/header context; not full source

L115 #### **The four tests: a framework for reading critically in the age of AI**

passages.text: Two weeks ago I gave Claude a detailed voice profile of my writing: sentence rhythm, rhetorical moves, vocabulary, the way I open with a blunt claim and close with a short sentence. I gave it access to my published posts. Then I asked it to write three excerpts on topics I have already covered, in my voice.

Excerpt 2, which is mine, contained the figure 19,797. The correct figure from my own published post is different (19,814). I copied the number incorrectly when preparing the excerpts and did not check before releasing the poll. Claude reproduced it without question.

I designed this experiment thinking the question was about detection. Your comments showed me the question is about evaluation. Detection asks: is this human or AI? Evaluation asks: is this any good, and how would you know?
That is the answer. Not whether Claude can write like me. But whether it can mean what I mean. It cannot. The question is whether you can tell the difference.

**How to apply it.** Before judging whether something was written by AI, ask whether the genre itself permits distinctiveness. A press release, a policy brief, and a corporate email are supposed to sound interchangeable. Evaluating them for ‘voice’ is a category error. Apply the omissions, necessity, and inhabitation tests instead. If those fail too, it does not matter who wrote it. The text is not doing the work of thinking.
No single test is definitive. A text can pass one and fail another. The framework is strongest when all four are applied together:
